claim: Anatomical models of memory have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix over the last 50 years.
source: Over the last 50 years, anatomical models of memory have repeatedly highlighted the hippocampal inputs to the mammillary bodies via the postcommissural fornix.
evidence: This is a statement about the historical focus of anatomical models, supported by established scientific literature and consensus in the field.

claim: Anatomical models of memory downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
source: Such models downplay other projections to the mammillary bodies, leaving them largely ignored.
evidence: This is an inference based on the historical emphasis on hippocampal inputs described in the manuscript.

claim: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests reported in the manuscript.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
source: Only mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions impaired behavioral tests of spatial working memory and, in particular, disrupted the use of extramaze spatial landmarks.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from behavioral tests in the study.

claim: Mammillothalamic tract and Gudden's ventral tegmental nucleus lesions produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data measuring c-fos expression presented in the manuscript.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions did not produce widespread reductions in c-fos expression in memory-related regions.
source: The same lesions also produced widespread reductions in immediate-early gene (c-fos) expression in a network of memory-related regions, not seen after postcommissural fornix lesions.
evidence: This is supported by immunohistochemical data comparing different lesion groups.

claim: The findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function dominated by hippocampal inputs.
source: These findings are inconsistent with previous models of mammillary body function (those dominated by hippocampal inputs) and herald a new understanding of why specific diencephalic structures are vital for memory.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data that showed postcommissural fornix lesions did not impair memory while other lesions did.

claim: The mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei.
source: Consequently, the mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei and, from there, to the cingulate (Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969) and prefrontal (Warrington and Weiskrantz, 1982) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature describing this model.

claim: The mammillary bodies relay hippocampal projections to the cingulate cortex.
source: Consequently, the mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei and, from there, to the cingulate (Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969) and prefrontal (Warrington and Weiskrantz, 1982) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The mammillary bodies relay hippocampal projections to the prefrontal cortex.
source: Consequently, the mammillary bodies are principally seen as a relay of hippocampal projections to the anterior thalamic nuclei and, from there, to the cingulate (Barbizet, 1963; Delay and Brion, 1969) and prefrontal (Warrington and Weiskrantz, 1982) cortices.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of an 'extended hippocampal system' is supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005), along with clinical evidence of the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus, via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Vann and Aggleton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical and clinical studies.

claim: Clinical evidence supports the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus via the mammillothalamic tract.
source: The notion that the mammillary bodies form part of such an 'extended hippocampal system' (Aggleton and Brown, 1999) is seemingly supported by the unidirectional nature of the hippocampal projections to the mammillary bodies (Aggleton et al., 2005), along with clinical evidence of the importance for memory of the mammillary body projections to the thalamus, via the mammillothalamic tract (MTT; Carlesimo et al., 2007; Van der Werf et al., 2000; Vann and Aggleton, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical studies.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function provide no real function for the mammillary bodies.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is a critical inference about the limitations of existing models.

claim: Standard models of mammillary body function ignore other mammillary body afferents.
source: However, these standard models suffer two major shortcomings. First, they provide no real function for the mammillary bodies and second, they ignore other mammillary body afferents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the focus of existing models on hippocampal inputs.

claim: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei.
source: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 1985), making it possible that these midbrain inputs are functionally important for memory (Vann, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: Midbrain inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei may be functionally important for memory.
source: The mammillary bodies receive dense inputs from Gudden's tegmental nuclei (e.g., Takeuchi et al., 1985), making it possible that these midbrain inputs are functionally important for memory (Vann, 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions disconnect the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact.
source: In one group the descending postcommissural fornix (PCF) was lesioned, a procedure that disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact, including those with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work describing this lesion method.

claim: Postcommissural fornix lesions leave hippocampal connections with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei intact.
source: In one group the descending postcommissural fornix (PCF) was lesioned, a procedure that disconnects the hippocampal formation projections to the mammillary bodies whilst leaving other hippocampal connections intact, including those with the septum, striatum and anterior thalamic nuclei (Vann et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous anatomical work.

claim: The lateral mammillary nucleus receives dense inputs from Gudden's dorsal tegmental nucleus.

evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.
